adventure.title: Secrets of St. George Street
adventure.description: A fictional merchant's ledger has been scattered among the shops and lanes of the historic district. Players must recover its pages by locating unusual products, signs, storefront details, local flavors, and hidden clues. St. George Street — named for King George III during the British colonial period — is the oldest commercial corridor in the oldest city in the United States. Its storefronts conceal stories from the Spanish colonial era through the Gilded Age.
adventure.short_description: Recover the missing merchant's ledger hidden among St. George Street's shops and signs.

stops.title: City Gate — The Ledger's First Page
stops.description: Every merchant who entered the colonial city passed through the City Gate — the two white coquina pillars at the north end of St. George Street that have framed the city's commercial entrance since 1808. The merchant's ledger begins here, with a note: 'To find the scattered pages, enter the street named for a king who never visited, and follow the clues left in stone, sign, and window.' St. George Street is named for King George III — the only British colonial landmark in St. Augustine that nearly every visitor experiences today.
stops.historical_content:
The City Gate was built in 1808 under Engineer Captain Manuel de Hita. The two coquina pillars (14 feet high, 12-foot opening) replaced the wooden La Leche Gate that had stood since 1739. Each pillar is topped with a pomegranate — the symbol of fertility and of Granada, Spain.

St. George Street was named during the British colonial period (1763-1784) for King George III of Britain. It replaced the earlier Spanish name for the same street. The street has been the primary commercial and residential corridor of St. Augustine since the early colonial period — under three national flags.

The pedestrian zone on St. George Street was created in the 20th century to protect the historic district from vehicle traffic. The reconstruction and preservation of the street's 18th-century character began in the 1950s with the St. Augustine Historical Restoration and Preservation Commission.

Under the Spanish, St. George Street housed colonial officials, merchants, and craftsmen. Under the British, it was lined with taverns and boarding houses. Under American rule, it became the primary tourist and shopping corridor — a role it has held continuously since the late 19th century.
stops.hint_text: Start at the City Gate — the two white coquina pillars at the north end of the St. George Street pedestrian zone. Face south to look down the street.

key_facts: City Gate built 1808 by Engineer Captain Manuel de Hita
Coquina pillars 14 feet high; opening 12 feet wide; each topped with a pomegranate
St. George Street named during the British period (1763-1784) for King George III
George III never visited St. Augustine — or North America
The street has been the primary commercial corridor under three national flags
Pedestrian zone created in the 20th century; historical restoration began 1950s

challenges.title: Named for a King Who Never Came
challenges.prompt: St. George Street was named during the British colonial period for a specific British monarch. But there's an irony in this naming. Which best describes it?
challenges.hint_text: The king after whom the street was named ruled a large empire — but never personally visited his American colonies.

options: King George III had personally surveyed the street during his visit to Florida in 1766
King George III gave the street its name in a royal decree, though he never visited St. Augustine or North America
The street was named after the patron saint George, not any king
King George III is buried in St. Augustine, making the name a memorial
config.explanation: King George III — for whom the street was named during Britain's Florida Period (1763-1784) — never visited St. Augustine or North America. The irony is that the most-walked street in the oldest American city is named for a king who never set foot in the Americas. The street's Spanish colonial name was replaced with the British one; the British name survived.

challenges.title: The Gate's Crown
challenges.prompt: Each of the two City Gate pillars is topped with a carved fruit — a symbol of both fertility and the city of Granada, Spain. What fruit tops each pillar?
challenges.hint_text: It's a fruit with a tough red skin and many seeds inside — used in Mediterranean cooking and as a symbol of abundance.

config.explanation: A pomegranate tops each pillar — the symbol of fertility and of Granada, Spain. The pomegranate is also connected to the city's Spanish heritage: Granada, the Spanish city, takes its name from the pomegranate (granada in Spanish).

challenges.title: Bonus: The Colonial Shopkeeper's Market
challenges.prompt: Ask the colonial shopkeeper what St. George Street looked like as a colonial commercial street — what kinds of shops were here, who the customers were, and how commerce worked before credit cards and refrigeration.
challenges.hint_text: Ask about what goods were imported via the situado, or what local crafts and products were made in the colonial city.

stops.title: St. Photios Shrine — The Second Page
stops.description: The second page of the merchant's ledger is hidden at the St. Photios Greek Orthodox National Shrine — the only Byzantine-style facade on St. George Street. The shrine commemorates the Greek and Minorcan immigrants who arrived in Florida in 1768. The clue on this page: 'Look for the building where one Mediterranean island meets the Florida sun, where the taste of the ancient world found new earth.' The Minorcans brought their food, language, and culture to this street — and some of that heritage survives in local shops today.
stops.historical_content:
The St. Photios Greek Orthodox National Shrine was established at 41 St. George Street in 1982 to commemorate the 1768 arrival of Greek, Minorcan, and Italian immigrants recruited by Dr. Andrew Turnbull. The building's Byzantine-style exterior makes it visually distinctive on St. George Street.

The Minorcan cultural heritage is visible in St. Augustine's commercial landscape: datil pepper hot sauces, Minorcan clam chowder ingredients, and Mediterranean-influenced ceramics and textiles are sold throughout the historic district. The datil pepper — grown almost exclusively in St. Johns County — appears in many products sold in St. George Street shops.

The Minorcan language (a dialect of Catalan) was spoken in St. Augustine into the early 20th century. Surnames on St. George Street storefronts sometimes reflect Minorcan heritage: Pacetti, Pellicer, Ponce, Usina, and Manucy are among the Minorcan family names still found in St. Augustine.
stops.hint_text: Walk south on St. George Street to number 41 — look for the Byzantine-style facade with the blue and white signage of the St. Photios Greek Orthodox National Shrine.
stops.safety_warning: The shrine is an active religious site. Photography may be restricted inside.

key_facts: St. Photios Shrine established 1982 at 41 St. George Street
Commemorates the 1768 arrival of Greek, Minorcan, and Italian immigrants
Byzantine-style exterior is unique on St. George Street
Minorcan datil pepper products are widely sold in historic district shops
Minorcan language (Catalan dialect) was spoken in St. Augustine into the early 20th century
Minorcan surnames still found in St. Augustine: Pacetti, Pellicer, Ponce, Usina, Manucy

challenges.title: Find the Datil
challenges.prompt: The Minorcans' most enduring contribution to St. Augustine's commercial landscape is a product sold in shops throughout the historic district. Which product — made from a pepper variety grown almost exclusively in St. Johns County, Florida — is the clearest sign of Minorcan heritage on St. George Street today?
challenges.hint_text: Look in any hot sauce or specialty food shop on St. George Street — you'll find this pepper's name on multiple products.

options: Jalapeño-based Florida hot sauce
Datil pepper hot sauce and seasoning
Minorcan olive oil
Citrus marmalade from Spanish colonial citrus trees
config.explanation: Datil pepper hot sauce — made from the Capsicum chinense pepper variety brought to Florida by the Minorcan immigrants in 1768 — is sold throughout St. George Street's shops. The datil pepper is grown almost exclusively in St. Johns County and is considered one of St. Augustine's signature products.

challenges.title: Window Shopping Detective
challenges.prompt: The merchant's ledger page says: 'Find a shop that sells something made locally from an ingredient unique to this county.' Walk into or past any shop on St. George Street selling local food products. Name the pepper that is unique to St. Johns County — the ingredient that makes local products here different from anywhere else in the world.
challenges.hint_text: It was brought by the Minorcans in 1768, grown almost nowhere else, and appears in the name of many local hot sauces and food products.

config.explanation: The datil pepper — Capsicum chinense, related to the habanero — is grown almost exclusively in St. Johns County, Florida. Brought by the Minorcan immigrants in 1768, it is the defining local ingredient of St. Augustine cooking and appears in dozens of locally made products sold on St. George Street.

challenges.title: Bonus: The Surviving Language
challenges.prompt: Ask the colonial shopkeeper about the Minorcan language — a dialect of Catalan that was spoken in St. Augustine into the early 20th century. What happened to it, and what other traces of Minorcan culture survive in the city's commercial life today?
challenges.hint_text: Ask about Minorcan family names in St. Augustine, or about what it means that a Mediterranean language survived in Florida for 150 years.

stops.title: Cathedral Area — The Third Page
stops.description: The third page of the merchant's ledger turns up near the Cathedral Basilica — the oldest Catholic parish in the United States. The ledger page reads: 'From the bell tower's shadow to the constitution stone, count what was built to stand forever and what was built to sell.' The contrast between the 18th-century permanence of the Cathedral and the constantly changing shopfronts of the surrounding commercial district tells the story of St. Augustine's dual identity: a city of historical monuments and a city of commerce.
stops.historical_content:
The Cathedral Basilica of St. Augustine was started in 1793 and dedicated December 8, 1797. Its reconstruction of 1887 (after a fire) preserved the original Spanish colonial mission facade but added a new bell tower. The cathedral's location at the plaza corner — facing the commercial district — reflects the Spanish colonial urban planning principle that church and commerce should share the same central space.

The commercial district around the Cathedral has changed radically over the centuries: Spanish colonial merchants, British colonial tavern-keepers, Gilded Age souvenir sellers, and modern tourism-focused retailers have all worked these same blocks. What has remained constant is the Cathedral's bell tower — visible from nearly every point in the historic district.

The Constitution Monument in the Plaza — erected 1813, survived the transfer to American rule because Mayor Geronimo Alvarez refused to remove it — stands as the only monument honoring the Spanish Constitution of 1812 in the Western Hemisphere. It is a direct contradiction to the commercial impermanence around it: a stone monument to a political document that most Americans have never heard of, standing in the middle of a tourist plaza.
stops.hint_text: Walk to the Cathedral Basilica on Cathedral Place — the church facing the Plaza de la Constitución. The Constitution Monument is in the adjacent plaza.
stops.safety_warning: Please be respectful near the Cathedral. Mass may be in progress.

key_facts: Cathedral started 1793; dedicated December 8, 1797 (Feast of the Immaculate Conception)
1887 fire led to reconstruction; Spanish colonial mission facade preserved; bell tower added
Bell tower is visible from nearly every point in the historic district
Constitution Monument (1813) stands in the plaza — only monument honoring the Spanish Constitution of 1812 in the Western Hemisphere
Mayor Geronimo Alvarez refused American officials' request to remove the monument after Florida's transfer in 1821

challenges.title: The Monument Nobody Knows
challenges.prompt: The Constitution Monument in the Plaza de la Constitución has a unique historical distinction. What makes it significant beyond St. Augustine?
challenges.hint_text: It honors a specific document that most Americans have never heard of — and it's the only monument of its kind surviving in the entire Western Hemisphere.

options: It is the only monument in North America built during Spanish colonial rule that has never been moved
It is the only surviving monument honoring the Spanish Constitution of 1812 in the Western Hemisphere
It is the oldest monument in the United States, predating all others by at least 50 years
It marks the exact spot where Florida's founding document was signed in 1565
config.explanation: The Constitution Monument (1813) is the only surviving monument honoring the Spanish Constitution of 1812 in the Western Hemisphere. Mayor Geronimo Alvarez refused American officials' requests to remove it when Florida transferred to the United States on July 10, 1821. The Spanish Constitution of 1812 established constitutional monarchy in Spain and was an inspiration for liberal movements across the Atlantic world.

challenges.title: The Bell Tower Landmark
challenges.prompt: The Cathedral Basilica's bell tower is visible from nearly every point in the historic district. But the original cathedral started in 1793 did not have this bell tower — it was added after a damaging event in 1887. What happened to the Cathedral in 1887 that required its reconstruction?
challenges.hint_text: It was a common disaster for 19th-century buildings, especially ones with wooden interiors.

config.explanation: The Cathedral was damaged by fire in 1887 — the same year Henry Flagler began his transformation of St. Augustine with the Ponce de León Hotel construction. The 1887 reconstruction preserved the original Spanish colonial mission facade but added the distinctive bell tower that now serves as a landmark visible from across the historic district.

challenges.title: Bonus: Trade and Faith
challenges.prompt: Ask the colonial shopkeeper about the relationship between the Cathedral and the market — in the Spanish colonial plaza design, the church and the commercial district shared the same central space. How did the Church and commerce coexist (or conflict) in colonial St. Augustine?
challenges.hint_text: Ask about Sunday markets, or about what merchants could and couldn't sell in a Spanish Catholic colonial city.

stops.title: Treasury Street Intersection — The Ledger's Secret Compartment
stops.description: The intersection of St. George Street and Treasury Street — one of the narrowest intersections in the historic district — is where the merchant's ledger has its most cryptic entry: 'Where the narrowest lane meets the widest commerce, the secret is in the sign you almost walked past.' Treasury Street was named for the Spanish Royal Treasury (Tesorero Real) whose office was nearby. It is one of several street names in St. Augustine that preserve the colonial administrative geography of the 18th-century city.
stops.historical_content:
Treasury Street was named for the Spanish Royal Treasury — the office of the Tesorero Real, which managed the colonial finances and the annual situado supply from Havana. The Tesorero's office was near the Government House on the plaza. Treasury Street connected the commercial St. George Street to the administrative area of the city.

St. Augustine's street names preserve three periods of colonial history:
- Spanish period names: Treasury Street (Calle del Tesoro), Bridge Street, Aviles Street
- British period names: St. George Street (named for King George III), King Street
- American period additions: Orange Street, Cordova Street

The width of colonial streets was regulated by Spanish colonial law — wider streets were required near the plaza and cathedral; narrower lanes served residential areas. Treasury Street's narrowness reflects its secondary commercial character in the colonial hierarchy.

The 'sign you almost walked past' refers to the observation challenge in this stop: finding the historical marker or building name that reveals the street's colonial administrative connection.
stops.hint_text: Walk south on St. George Street to the intersection with Treasury Street — the narrow east-west lane just south of the Cathedral. Look for historical markers and street signs.

key_facts: Treasury Street named for the Spanish Royal Treasury (Tesorero Real) office nearby
Street names in St. Augustine preserve three periods: Spanish (Aviles, Treasury), British (St. George, King), American (Orange, Cordova)
Colonial street widths were regulated by Spanish law — wider near plazas, narrower in residential areas
The Tesorero Real managed the situado, the annual colonial financial subsidy from Havana
Juan Esteban de Peña (who built the Peña-Peck House) held the Tesorero Real position

challenges.title: Decoding the Street Names
challenges.prompt: St. Augustine's street names preserve three periods of colonial history. Which street name is a survival from the BRITISH colonial period (1763-1784)?
challenges.hint_text: The British named streets after their own monarchs and institutions. One of St. Augustine's most famous streets carries a British colonial name.

options: Aviles Street
Treasury Street
St. George Street
Bridge Street
config.explanation: St. George Street was named during the British colonial period (1763-1784) for King George III. Aviles Street was named for the hometown of St. Augustine's Spanish founder Pedro Menéndez de Avilés. Treasury Street comes from the Spanish Royal Treasury (Tesorero Real). Bridge Street was named for the colonial-era bridge over the Sebastian River.

challenges.title: The Office That Funded the City
challenges.prompt: Treasury Street is named for the colonial office that managed St. Augustine's finances. What was the annual financial subsidy — sent from Havana and ultimately from Mexico City — that kept the city solvent called?
challenges.hint_text: The Spanish word for this subsidy is also the word for the financial situation of being provided for or maintained.

config.explanation: The situado was the annual subsidy sent from Mexico City via Havana to fund St. Augustine's colonial government, soldiers, church, and population. Without it, the city could not have survived — St. Augustine produced no significant export crop or trade income. The Tesorero Real (Royal Treasurer), whose office gave Treasury Street its name, was responsible for receiving and distributing the situado.

challenges.title: Bonus: The Merchant's Route
challenges.prompt: Ask the colonial shopkeeper about the merchant's daily route through the historic district — from the City Gate, down St. George Street, past the Cathedral, and through the Treasury Street intersection. What would have been in each shop, and how did prices work in a colonial economy?
challenges.hint_text: Ask about barter, credit, or what a colonial merchant's most valuable products were.

stops.title: Government House — The Ledger's Final Page
stops.description: The final page of the merchant's ledger is at Government House — the seat of power that has overlooked St. George Street's commerce for over 400 years. The ledger's final entry reads: 'The merchant records what passes through; the government records what is taxed. Both have kept records from this street since before any nation remembered it.' Government House's history as a commercial regulator — taxing imports, monitoring trade, issuing licenses — is the hidden story behind St. George Street's commercial character.
stops.historical_content:
Government House at 48 King Street has been the center of governmental administration in St. Augustine since 1598 — when the first Governors' House was built on this site. Under every colonial power, Government House regulated trade: setting tariffs, licensing merchants, adjudicating commercial disputes, and controlling imports.

The Spanish colonial commercial system was heavily regulated: merchants needed licenses to operate; imported goods were subject to tariffs; the Church had rules about what could be sold on Sundays and feast days. The situado (annual supply) was the main commercial transaction of the colonial economy — government-to-government rather than merchant-to-consumer.

During the British period, St. George Street became more commercially active — British colonial administration was less restrictive of private trade. Taverns, boarding houses, and private merchants expanded their operations.

After American rule began in 1821, Government House became a federal courthouse and post office — continuing its role as the administrative center while St. George Street commercialized rapidly through the 19th century.

The current building dates mostly from the 1834-36 reconstruction, when it was rebuilt in Greek Revival style for the American territorial government. The original Spanish colonial building was demolished, but the site has not changed.
stops.hint_text: Government House is on King Street at the northwest corner of the Plaza de la Constitución — the large building with a covered walkway facing the plaza.

key_facts: Government House site in use as center of government since 1598 — oldest continuous government site in the United States
Spanish colonial commerce was heavily regulated: merchant licenses, tariffs, Sunday trading restrictions
British period allowed more commercial freedom; St. George Street became more active
After 1821: federal courthouse and post office
Current building dates to 1834-36 reconstruction in Greek Revival style
Site has never changed even as the building has been rebuilt multiple times

challenges.title: The Longest Government
challenges.prompt: Government House has been the center of governmental administration in St. Augustine since 1598 — under Spanish, British, Confederate, and American rule. What makes this site uniquely significant in American governmental history?
challenges.hint_text: Think about how long this site has been in continuous government use compared to any other location in what is now the United States.

options: It is the location where Florida's state constitution was written in 1822
It is the site of the only surviving Spanish colonial government building in North America
It has been in continuous use as a seat of government longer than any other site in what is now the United States — since 1598
It was the building where the Treaty of Paris (1763) was signed, transferring Florida to Britain
config.explanation: Government House has been the center of governmental administration since 1598 — making it the longest continuously used government site in what is now the United States. The building has been rebuilt multiple times under different colonial powers, but the site itself has never changed administrative function.

challenges.title: The Ledger's Final Entry
challenges.prompt: You've recovered all the pages of the merchant's ledger. For the final entry, answer: What year did Florida transfer from Spanish to American rule — with the flags exchanged in the plaza you can see from Government House?
challenges.hint_text: The Adams-Onís Treaty was signed in 1819 and ratified in 1821. The actual flags-exchange ceremony happened in the year of ratification.

config.explanation: Florida transferred from Spain to the United States on July 10, 1821 — with the flags exchanged in the Plaza de la Constitución. Governor José Coppinger lowered the Spanish flag; Andrew Jackson raised the American one. The merchant's ledger — which had recorded trade under Spanish, British, and territorial American governments — closed one chapter and opened another.

challenges.title: Bonus: The Ledger Completed
challenges.prompt: Ask the colonial shopkeeper to complete the merchant's story — what happened to the merchants of St. George Street after Florida became an American territory in 1821? Did the street prosper, decline, or change character?
challenges.hint_text: Ask about Henry Flagler's effect on the commercial district in the 1880s, or about what the street looked like before the tourist economy developed.
